I can tell, because I have the ability to do things I otherwise wouldn't want to or would put myself at risk of doing. Something which would not occur in natural systems whose primary purpose is survival and reproduction. For instance, I can go jump out of an airplane and run the risk of dying with a parachute failure, or I can chose to not date, marry, and breed. Both are contrary to our biologically evolved purposes, and not something that would be trait selected for. It is emergent behavior.

Obviously this emergent behavior is a direct result of our brains and neurochemistry, despite having evolved for simpler purposes (motor function, etc).

I agree that a process in your brain can lead to behaviors that are suboptimal for reproduction. I don't see how that supports the notion of free will though. If biology could be fallible enough to evolve free will (which could lead to bad outcomes as you described) couldn't it have created equally flawed deterministic systems?

It's pretty simple really. Free will isn't deterministic simply because it can't be. There are no physical systems governing it to violate, despite being a product of them.

You can think of free will as a virtual machine running on the universe's hardware. VMs, for example, can do things that the computer they are running on wouldn't normally be able to (like emulate other systems). This will especially be the case if we can conclusively prove the multiple-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, as human choice would effectively create new world-tracks (realities) willy-nilly.

Causality doesn't have to be absolutely deterministic (Copenhagen interpretation). If it were, it would make more sense for all living creatures to be empty mindless drones since physics tends to produce results through the most simple means possible and would likely see the universe employ a deterministic system to govern human behavior (some observable effect). With MWI, we still have causality and the rational capability for free-will is preserved, fate need not apply. Instead of everything collapsing to a single eigenstate, we just end up with an infinite myriad of ones which become no longer accessible to us.

Which makes more sense given the fact that our natural universe itself has [created/brought about/resulted in] non-deterministic systems within it. Radioactive decay and electron behavior are both such cases and fundamental components of the universe. So it's not like the two things can't coexist naturally, because they do.

I'm self-evidently not an automaton simply mechanically reproducing a predetermined string of words - instead, I'm a thinking creature, deliberately choosing specific words at specific times - entertaining some, choosing some, rejecting some - deciding, at every step of the way, rather than merely reproducing that which was set in motion when the first atom collided with the second atom.

And my day, and more to the point, your day, is absolutely stuffed to the brim with those moments - with those subjective experiences of that which we call "free will."

How so?

A given effect doesn't have a single cause, nor is it ever really a simple and monolithic chain. That's a misleading oversimplification. A given effect has any number of interconnected causes - an enormous and generally indecipherable web of interdependent causes and effects and causes and effects. I don't see how the introduction of a single additional cause to that chain in any way "violates causality," and in fact the mere fact that each chain is already composed of countless interconnected causes and effects clearly means that the addition of additional causes and additional effects to an existing chain doesn't "violate causality" - it simply alters the possible outcomes.

I think that the mistake that people make regarding free will is to first declare it to be somehow outside of the chain of cause and effect, then declare that since nothing can be outside of the chain of cause and effect, therefore it can't exist.
